original.reason: The Case 2 claim that p^2 cannot divide n is false: p^2 may divide n when q<p^2, as the proposed n=2009 itself shows (49 divides 2009 and 41<49). More importantly, checking p=2,3,5,7 does not prove that no larger prime p can occur; no bound or exhaustive argument is supplied.

judgment.reason: The asserted classification lemma is not proved. Saying to factor p^3-15 and check possibilities does not provide a finite exhaustive argument over all primes p.
The central 'standard two-prime divisor lemma' is merely invoked, not established. Its claimed complete check lacks a bound or argument covering every prime p.
The necessary classification lemma is only described informally. No proof eliminates all possible primes p and q, so uniqueness is unsupported.
The proof depends entirely on an unproved 'two-prime divisor lemma.' Factoring p^3-15 for an unspecified prime p is not an exhaustive proof.
